q: Entering a Mediterranean harbour from seaward you see this buoy. Which side do you leave it on?
why: Region A: red can to port when returning.

q: This mark is ahead. Where is the safe water?
why: North cardinal: black over yellow, both cones up.

q: You see this mark. Which way round do you go?
answer: Keep clear, but you may pass on any side
why: Isolated danger: black with red bands, two balls; danger right under it.

q: This buoy is at the harbour approach. What does it tell you?
answer: Safe water all round — a landfall or mid-channel mark
why: Red and white vertical stripes, red ball: safe water.

q: A yellow buoy with this topmark sits off the beach. What is it?
answer: A special mark — check the chart (swimming area, pipeline, spoil ground)
why: Yellow with an X: not a navigation mark in itself.

q: Leaving the marina at Kalamata for the open sea, you have this buoy ahead. On which side do you leave it?
why: Region A: a green cone marks the starboard side going in, so it stays on your port side going out.

figure.note: You are heading out to sea

q: You are returning to Road Town, Tortola (BVI), from sea. This buoy is ahead. Which side do you leave it?
why: Region B (the Americas): red, conical, kept to starboard returning — "red right returning".

q: Entering English Harbour, Antigua, from the sea, you see this buoy. What is it?
answer: A port-hand mark: leave it to port
why: Region B: green and can-shaped marks the port side when entering.

figure.note: IALA region B · entering from sea

ru.IALA region B · entering from sea: МАМС, регион В · вход с моря

q: Sailing along the coast of Lefkada, you see this mark. On which side of it is the safe water?
why: East cardinal: black–yellow–black, cones base to base; pass to the east.

q: This mark stands off a reef near Hvar. Where do you pass it?
why: West cardinal: yellow–black–yellow, cones point to point; safe water to the west.

q: Sailing in the Bahamas (IALA region B), you see this mark. What does it mean there?
answer: Pass to the east, as in region A
why: Only lateral marks differ between regions A and B; cardinals are the same worldwide.

q: Rounding a headland in the Gulf of Corinth, you see this mark off the point. Where is the danger?
why: South cardinal: safe water to the south, so the danger lies to the north of it.

q: Anchoring off a beach in Zakynthos, you see a line of these buoys between you and the shore. What do they usually mark?
answer: The edge of a swimming area: stay outside
why: Yellow special marks along beaches usually mark the bathing zone; check the chart or local rules.

figure.note: Small buoys in a line parallel to the beach

ru.Small buoys in a line parallel to the be: Небольшие буйки в линию вдоль пляжа

q: Off Piraeus you see this new buoy, which is not on your chart. What does it mark?
answer: A recent wreck, not yet charted
why: Blue and yellow stripes: an emergency wreck-marking buoy over a new, uncharted wreck.

q: You see two of these marks close together where your up-to-date chart shows clear water. What does it mean?
answer: A newly found danger, marked with a duplicate
why: IALA: a serious new danger may be marked by duplicating one of the marks until it is charted.

figure.note: Two of these, side by side; chart shows clear water
